perspectives.title: Why does India’s chip ambition keep running into fire, malware, and paperwork? Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw’s recent warning about calculated disruptions and cyberattacks targeting Indian manufacturing wasn’t rhetorical. It described a pattern that’s played out for four decades. Strategic industries rarely get challenged with open hostility. They get challenged with friction that’s technically explainable and diplomatically unattributable. Every new entrant into chips, rare earths, or critical minerals learns this eventually. That’s what makes India’s semiconductor mission more than an industrial policy question. It’s a test of whether a rising manufacturing power keeps building through exactly the kind of resistance incumbency always mounts against a new competitor. Vaishnaw’s warning is an acknowledgment: the friction is real, it’s patterned, and it isn’t going away. Accident, or something more deliberate? Tell me where you land.
